Tests are the most thorough of the three: parameterised invalid urls and codes, chunked 413, clock-injected window reset, a spawn test of server.mjs checking PORT, DB_FILE and ADMIN_TOKEN and persistence, and frontend render/init tests with a fake DOM whose innerHTML throws. Minor issues: src/http.mjs mixes unrelated concerns (JSON I/O, rate limiter, static serving). On 413 the rest of the body is drained instead of closing the connection. No test of an exact 10240-byte body. '//x' request paths parse 'x' as a host, a quirk shared by all three. The README is concise and accurate, with a configuration table, a PowerShell example, curl examples and a note on X-Forwarded-For.

reasoning: Z and X are close; Y is clearly behind. I ran each test suite in a temp copy (all pass: Z 54, X 34, Y 23) plus the same 100-case black-box probe and a few targeted probes. Z and X both passed all 100 probe cases; Y failed 3. Z ranks above X on spec fidelity. X always rewrites the redirect Location with new URL(url).href, so the redirect does not return the stored url: 'https://example.com' becomes 'https://example.com/', the host is lower-cased and the port and dot segments are dropped. An exact Location check on the most common input would fail. X also treats PORT='' as port 0, a random port. Z keeps the stored url verbatim and only percent-encodes urls that are not header-safe. Z also adds defence in depth (CSP, graceful shutdown that closes the DB) and has the stronger tests: fake-DOM tests of rendering and form wiring, and a spawned-server test of env config and persistence. X's tests are excellent on exact boundaries but leave DOM rendering and DB_FILE untested. Y ranks last because its validation is weak. It accepts url forms that are not absolute ('http:x', 'http:/x', leading spaces, embedded tab/CR/LF) and stores them raw. Its unencoded Location header then breaks: any url with non-Latin-1 characters (CJK, emoji) or CRLF returns 201 on create but 500 on every redirect. The Location header is percent-encoded through new URL().href (server.mjs:70), so non-ASCII and IDN targets redirect correctly. The token compare is constant-time over SHA-256 digests (server.mjs:29-34). Inserts rely on the PRIMARY KEY, so there is no check-then-insert race (store.mjs:45). The rate limiter caps each key at `limit` timestamps and prunes idle keys (rate-limit.mjs:17-25); 50k hits take 25 ms. No test shows data surviving a restart with DB_FILE. PORT='' becomes port 0 (server.mjs:128, Number('')), a minor quirk. Code-length acceptance at exactly 3 and 32 is not tested.

Y.notes: npm test: 23/23 pass. The core API matches the spec: 415/413/400/409/201/429 with every POST counted, stats, the DELETE order, the unset-token 401, static types, and the defaults. Defects found by probing: (1) URL validation is too lax (app.mjs:37-40, new URL only). It accepts ' http://a.com' with a leading space, 'http:a.com', 'http:/a.com', and URLs containing CR/LF, tab or space, and stores them verbatim. That violates 'absolute http:// or https:// URL'. (2) The redirect writes the raw stored string into Location (app.mjs:106). Any URL with characters outside Latin-1 (e.g. http://a.com/café/漢) and any stored CRLF URL give HTTP 500 'Invalid character in header content' after the click has already been counted. Latin-1, tab and space characters go out raw in the header, and IDN hosts are not punycoded. Creation accepted these links, then the redirect broke them. (3) The rate limiter (ratelimit.mjs:5-10) keeps every timestamp per key, so per-request cost is O(n) and growth is unbounded. 50k hits from one IP took 8.8 s of event-loop CPU, an amplification vector for denial of service. Idle keys are never pruned, which a comment acknowledges. (4) HEAD /<code> counts a click (app.mjs:124). (5) tokenOk leaks the token length through an early length check (app.mjs:47-48). Code is compact but dense: app.mjs packs validation, SQL and routing together, with one-line try/catch blocks. There is no app factory export, so every server test spawns a process. Tests are black-box and reasonable (21st POST is exactly the first 429, PORT=0 against a configured PORT, chunked 413, unset token). They do not check acceptance at the 2048-char or 10240-byte boundaries, never test unicode or whitespace URLs, and server.test's rate-limit test depends on test order and shared server state. Frontend tests cover only api.js. The README is clear, with curl examples and status tables. The UI worked in a browser.

Z.notes: npm test: 54/54 pass. Probing found the same full compliance as X: the 415/413/400 cases including chunked bodies, a declared 100 KB body and the exact 10240-byte body; 2048/2049; 3/32; 409; 429 on the 21st POST with rejected requests counted; stats; redirect with click count; DELETE 401/404/204 with unset or empty token; defaults. Strengths: strict URL validation (app.mjs:18-27) rejects whitespace and control characters, requires a non-empty hostname and rejects 'http:a.com'. Location is sent verbatim only when it is printable ASCII, otherwise as URL.href (app.mjs:16,91), so unicode and IDN targets redirect correctly. INSERT OR IGNORE plus changes===1 handles collisions without control flow by exception (store.mjs:28-44). The rate limiter is bounded (slice(-limit-1)), and an unref'd interval sweeps idle keys and is cleared on close (app.mjs:59, http.mjs:71-89). Bodies are drained on 415/413/429 so error responses arrive cleanly (http.mjs:33-40, app.mjs:64). It sends a CSP and nosniff on HTML, compares the token in constant time over SHA-256, and shuts down on SIGINT/SIGTERM. Tests are the broadest of the three: table-driven invalid URLs and codes, 3/32/2048 acceptance, chunked 413 through a ReadableStream, rate-limit reset with an injected clock, a check that GETs are not limited, non-ASCII redirect encoding, and DB_FILE persistence across a server restart. Frontend tests use a fake DOM whose innerHTML throws, so they cover rendering and the init() form wiring as well as the fetch logic. The README is concise and accurate (PowerShell example, coverage script, note that X-Forwarded-For is not trusted). Defects: http.mjs is a grab-bag (body reading, rate limiter and static serving in one module), and public/app.js mixes fetch and DOM code, though both are injectable. The UI has no busy or disabled state, so double submits are possible, and it shows createdAt as a raw ISO string. server.test.mjs picks a random port in 30000-50000, which can flake on Windows excluded ranges or on collisions. There is no test for the exact 10240-byte boundary and no network-failure test for the frontend. Wrong methods return 404 rather than 405, which the spec does not require.

reasoning: Z and X are close; Y is clearly last. In my probing, X and Z both met every explicit rule in the spec. Both reject malformed and whitespace URLs, percent-encode non-ASCII Location headers, cap rate-limiter memory, compare the admin token in constant time and block path traversal. Both frontends worked end to end in a real browser and use textContent only. Z ranks first for its stronger test suite: 54 tests versus 34. Its suite includes DOM-level frontend tests that exercise rendering and the init() form wiring, a DB_FILE persistence-across-restart test, and table-driven invalid-input cases with both-sided 3/32/2048 boundaries. Z also adds hardening X lacks: bodies drained on 413/415/429, a CSP header and graceful shutdown. X has the more polished UI (busy state, copy button, formatted dates), 405 handling, an exact-10240-byte body test and a slightly cleaner module split. That keeps it a near-tie, but its frontend tests stop at api.js. Y implements the happy path and the status codes correctly but has real defects. URL validation accepts leading spaces, 'http:a.com' and URLs containing CR/LF, tab or space, and stores them verbatim. Because the stored string goes straight into Location, redirects to non-Latin-1 or CRLF URLs return HTTP 500, after the click is counted. Its rate limiter grows without bound per key and is quadratic (8.8 s of CPU for 50k hits from one IP). Its tests are thinner and depend on test order, and miss the acceptance boundaries.

X.notes: All 25 tests pass. My probes found every spec line met: 415/413 (Content-Length and chunked)/400/409/429 ordering, a body of exactly 10240 bytes is accepted, generated 7-char code, short uses the real port, stats return a numeric clicks and an ISO createdAt, DELETE gives 401 when ADMIN_TOKEN is unset, 204 with an empty body, and traversal returns 404. It is the only solution that returns Content-Type exactly `application/json`. Strengths: one clear 244-line server.mjs with named constants. toHeaderSafeUrl (server.mjs:100-104) percent-encodes non-ASCII and control-character targets, so a unicode URL redirects correctly, and a test covers this. timingSafeEqual compares the token. The fetch logic in public/api.js is cleanly separated and tested with a fake fetch. Verified in a browser: shorten, 409 error and stats all render through textContent. Defects: (1) The rate limiter (server.mjs:57-69) keeps a timestamp for every POST, including 429s, then filters and copies that array on each request. Under a one-IP flood this is O(n^2): I measured 10k requests at 1.9 s CPU and 40k at 27 s, so the limiter itself becomes a DoS lever. Every request also scans the whole Map. (2) HEAD /<code> increments clicks (server.mjs:212-217). (3) It accepts 'http:example.com' and spaces in URLs, which WHATWG parsing allows but is loose. (4) No handling for a bad PORT or listen errors: the process crashes with a stack trace (server.mjs:238-243). (5) Oversized chunked bodies are read to the end instead of closing early (server.mjs:81-89). (6) public/app.js:16 sets href from API data without a scheme check (low risk). Tests miss chunked 413, the exact 2048-character boundary, rate-window expiry and HEAD. The README is concise and accurate, including the limits of the limiter and the client IP.

Y.notes: All 83 tests pass. My probes found every spec behaviour correct, including a unicode-URL redirect (encoded Location), a body of exactly 10240 bytes accepted with 10241 rejected, chunked 413, and DELETE returning 401 when the token is unset. Strengths: a clean modular split (lib/db, http, links, rate-limit, static) with a short router in server.mjs. Insertion is atomic (INSERT OR IGNORE plus changes, links.mjs:55-58), so there is no check-then-insert race. Control characters are rejected up front (links.mjs:9-21), which blocks CRLF in Location. Token comparison uses sha256 then timingSafeEqual, so even the length does not leak (links.mjs:68-73). The rate limiter is bounded to limit+1 timestamps with a sweep, and a 5000-request flood unit test with an injected clock covers it (rate-limit.mjs, input-hardening.test.mjs). On overflow the body read stops early and the response sends Connection: close (http.mjs:40-61). Every response carries nosniff, an invalid PORT exits with code 1 and a clear message, and the frontend safeHref allows only http(s) links. The UI was verified in a browser. Tests are the most thorough of the three: both 2048-character boundaries, codes of length 3 and 32, chunked 413, raw-path traversal, persistence across process restarts, CLI startup, the frontend api against the real server, and a DOM-sink scan. The README is extensive and accurate, covering check ordering, PowerShell usage and the project layout. Defects: index.html:7-9 loads Google Fonts, an external request and privacy leak for an otherwise self-contained app. A URL with a space is stored and sent as a raw space in Location (links.mjs:11,87). HEAD returns 405. JSON Content-Type carries a '; charset=utf-8' parameter, which is fine but not a literal match. backend-smoke.test.mjs largely duplicates api.test.mjs and has a weak `[200,404].includes` assertion (line 66), and its `limited.close()` is not awaited (line 84). It also accepts 'http:example.com'.

Z.notes: All 32 tests pass. Strengths: the strictest URL validation of the three (server.mjs:23): an explicit `^https?://`, a non-empty host, and whitespace and control characters rejected, so 'http:example.com' and URLs with spaces correctly get 400. Insertion is atomic, using the UNIQUE/PK errcode for 409, with a retry loop for generated codes (server.mjs:76-79,92-96). The rate limiter is bounded and checked before validation. Auth is checked before existence on DELETE. HEAD is supported without counting a click. Static serving, with stat/isFile and nosniff, is factored out. The tests are good: boundary 2048 accepted, exactly 20 POSTs allowed, chunked 413, CR/LF rejection, traversal against a temporary publicDir that holds a secret file, persistence, and a CLI integration test. The frontend was verified in a browser and uses textContent with an http(s)-only href check. Defects: (1) Real correctness bug: the redirect writes the stored URL raw into Location (server.mjs:125). A non-ASCII URL such as http://a.com/日本 is accepted with 201, but GET /<code> then returns 500 (ERR_INVALID_CHAR in stderr). The click was already counted by the UPDATE at line 123 before the failure. Latin-1 targets go out as raw high bytes. No test covers this. (2) An oversized chunked body is read to the end before the 413 is sent (server.mjs:37-41). (3) The code is dense: many long one-liners (server.mjs:23,39,72,83,130) make it harder to read than X or Y. (4) JSON Content-Type includes a charset parameter. (5) createServer defaults to ':memory:', which is fine since main passes DB_FILE. The README is accurate and practical, though it does not mention that the limiter is in-memory per process.

reasoning: All three pass their own suites and work end to end in a browser. Y ranks first. It meets every spec line I probed and is the most robust: bounded limiter, early 413 with the connection closed, control characters rejected, atomic insert, a constant-time token check that does not leak length, and non-ASCII redirects that work. It also has the clearest modular structure, the most thorough tests (boundaries, chunked 413, flood behaviour, process restarts) and the best README. Its flaws are minor: Google Fonts, a raw space allowed in Location, HEAD returning 405, and some redundant tests. X ranks second. Its correctness is clean (it is the only one with a literal application/json Content-Type, and it handles unicode redirects with a test), and its code is compact and readable. However, its rate limiter grows without bound and costs O(n^2) under a one-IP flood (27 s of CPU for 40k requests), HEAD counts clicks, and its tests are the thinnest. Z ranks last. It has the best URL validation, solid tests and atomic inserts, but a real functional bug: a URL with non-ASCII characters is accepted with 201, then the redirect fails with 500 after already counting a click. Its code is also the densest. I placed Z below X because Z's bug breaks the core redirect path for valid accepted input, while X's weakness only appears under abusive load.
